::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- reduce a data frame to summary statistics with `summarise()`, `n()` and `n_distinct()`;
- compute the same summaries **for each group** with `group_by()` or the `.by` argument;
- apply several functions to several columns at once with `across()` and control the names with `.names`;
- use grouped `mutate()` to compare each unit with its own group (e.g. centring within group);
- recognise and avoid the two classic pitfalls: missing values and grouped data "leaking" into later steps.
:::




::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```
:::


## 1. Why summarise?

A table with 344 penguins is too long to *read*. To answer questions like "are Gentoo penguins heavier than Adelie?" we need to **compress** many rows into a few numbers: a mean, a standard deviation, a count — one set of numbers for each species.

This is the first step of **descriptive statistics**: describing a variable with a few well-chosen summaries, separately for each group we want to compare. The statistics themselves (mean vs median, standard deviation, IQR…) are discussed in [Summary statistics](../05-descriptive/22-summary-statistics.qmd); here we learn the **tools** to compute them.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins <- as_tibble(penguins)
```
:::


## 2. `summarise()`: many rows to one


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   mean_mass
#>       <dbl>
#> 1        NA
```


:::
:::


The result is `NA`: two penguins have a missing body mass, and the mean of a set of numbers that includes an unknown number is unknown. We must say explicitly that missing values should be removed:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mass   = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    n         = n(),
    n_mass    = sum(!is.na(body_mass))
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   mean_mass sd_mass     n n_mass
#>       <dbl>   <dbl> <int>  <int>
#> 1     4202.   802.0   344    342
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- The output has **one row**, because we summarised the whole table, and one column per summary.
- `n()` counts **rows** (344), including those with a missing mass; `sum(!is.na(body_mass))` counts the **non-missing values** (342). The mean was computed on the second number — this is the sample size you should report.
:::

`summarise()` accepts any function that returns **one value**: `mean()`, `median()`, `sd()`, `min()`, `max()`, `quantile(x, 0.9)`, and also `n()` (number of rows) and `n_distinct()` (number of different values).

## 3. Summaries by group

The real power comes when we split the table into groups, summarise each group, and stack the results. This idea is called **split–apply–combine**.

### `group_by()` + `summarise()`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mass   = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    n         = n()
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   species   mean_mass sd_mass     n
#>   <fct>         <dbl>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Adelie        3701.   458.6   152
#> 2 Chinstrap     3733.   384.3    68
#> 3 Gentoo        5076.   504.1   124
```


:::
:::


Now there is **one row per species**. Gentoo penguins are about 1400 g heavier than Adelie on average. Whether such a difference could be due to chance is a question for [t-tests](../08-inference/34-t-tests.qmd).

### The `.by` argument

Since dplyr 1.1 you can group **for a single operation** with `.by`:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .by = species
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   species   mean_mass     n
#>   <fct>         <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Adelie        3701.   152
#> 2 Gentoo        5076.   124
#> 3 Chinstrap     3733.    68
```


:::
:::


The numbers are the same. Two differences: the result is **never grouped** afterwards (see section 6), and the groups appear in the order in which they first occur in the data, not alphabetically. Add `arrange(species)` if you need a sorted table.

### Several grouping variables


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  summarise(
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_len, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(species, sex)
  ) |>
  arrange(species, sex)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   species   sex    mean_flipper     n
#>   <fct>     <fct>         <dbl> <int>
#> 1 Adelie    female        187.8    73
#> 2 Adelie    male          192.4    73
#> 3 Chinstrap female        191.7    34
#> 4 Chinstrap male          199.9    34
#> 5 Gentoo    female        212.7    58
#> 6 Gentoo    male          221.5    61
```


:::
:::


Each row is now a **combination** of species and sex. Within every species males have longer flippers on average — an example of a pattern you can only see after grouping.

### `n_distinct()`


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    n_islands = n_distinct(island),
    n_years   = n_distinct(year),
    .by = species
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   species   n_islands n_years
#>   <fct>         <int>   <int>
#> 1 Adelie            3       3
#> 2 Gentoo            1       3
#> 3 Chinstrap         1       3
```


:::
:::


Only Adelie penguins were sampled on all three islands; keep this in mind before comparing islands, because island and species are **confounded** (mixed together).

## 4. Many columns at once: `across()`

Typing `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` for every column is tedious and error-prone. `across()` applies one or more functions to a set of columns:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    across(starts_with("bill"), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .by = species
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   species   bill_len bill_dep
#>   <fct>        <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie       38.79    18.35
#> 2 Gentoo       47.50    14.98
#> 3 Chinstrap    48.83    18.42
```


:::
:::


The first argument of `across()` selects columns (with any of the helpers from `select()`); the second is the function. `\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)` is an **anonymous function**: "take a column `x` and return its mean without missing values".

With **several functions**, give them names in a list; `.names` builds the column names from the column (`{.col}`) and the function name (`{.fn}`):


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(bill_len, flipper_len),
      list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
           sd   = \(x) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    ),
    .by = species
  )
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   species   bill_len_mean bill_len_sd flipper_len_mean flipper_len_sd
#>   <fct>             <dbl>       <dbl>            <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie            38.79       2.663            190.0          6.539
#> 2 Gentoo            47.50       3.082            217.2          6.485
#> 3 Chinstrap         48.83       3.339            195.8          7.132
```


:::
:::


`across()` also works inside `mutate()`, for example to round every numeric column: `mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1)))`. It replaces the old `summarise_at()`, `mutate_if()` and similar functions, which you may still see in older code.

## 5. Grouped `mutate()`: comparing a unit with its group

`summarise()` returns one row per group. `mutate()` with groups keeps **all rows**, but computes group statistics for each row. A typical use is **centring within group**: how much heavier is each penguin than the average of its own species?


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
centred <- penguins |>
  mutate(
    species_mean  = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    mass_centred  = body_mass - species_mean,
    .by = species
  ) |>
  select(species, body_mass, species_mean, mass_centred)

centred
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 344 × 4
#>    species body_mass species_mean mass_centred
#>    <fct>       <int>        <dbl>        <dbl>
#>  1 Adelie       3750        3701.        49.34
#>  2 Adelie       3800        3701.        99.34
#>  3 Adelie       3250        3701.      -450.7 
#>  4 Adelie         NA        3701.        NA   
#>  5 Adelie       3450        3701.      -250.7 
#>  6 Adelie       3650        3701.       -50.66
#>  7 Adelie       3625        3701.       -75.66
#>  8 Adelie       4675        3701.       974.3 
#>  9 Adelie       3475        3701.      -225.7 
#> 10 Adelie       4250        3701.       549.3 
#> # ℹ 334 more rows
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read this output

- `species_mean` is the same for all penguins of a species — it is repeated on every row.
- `mass_centred` is positive for penguins heavier than their species average, negative for lighter ones. Within each species, its mean is zero (up to rounding).
- A Gentoo with `mass_centred = 0` is "average for a Gentoo", even though it is much heavier than any average Adelie. Centring removes differences *between* groups to focus on variation *within* groups.
:::

Other common grouped mutates: the share of each unit in its group total (`x / sum(x)`), the rank within group (`min_rank(desc(x))`), or a **z-score within group** (`(x - mean(x)) / sd(x)`), which you will meet again in descriptive statistics.

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: within- and between-group variation

Write $x_{ij}$ for the mass of penguin $i$ in species $j$, $\bar x_j$ for the species mean and $\bar x$ for the overall mean. Then

$$
x_{ij} - \bar x \;=\; \underbrace{(\bar x_j - \bar x)}_{\text{between groups}} \;+\; \underbrace{(x_{ij} - \bar x_j)}_{\text{within group (centred)}} .
$$

Summing the squares of each part over all penguins splits the total variability into a between-group and a within-group part. This decomposition is the heart of [ANOVA](../08-inference/37-anova.qmd).
:::

## 6. Grouped data frames and `ungroup()`

`group_by()` attaches the grouping **to the data frame**, and it stays there. This is convenient, but it is also the source of a subtle bug. Suppose we want the proportion of each species–sex combination among *all* penguins:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#> # Groups:   species [3]
#>   species   sex        n   prop
#>   <fct>     <fct>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie    female    73 0.5   
#> 2 Adelie    male      73 0.5   
#> 3 Chinstrap female    34 0.5   
#> 4 Chinstrap male      34 0.5   
#> 5 Gentoo    female    58 0.4874
#> 6 Gentoo    male      61 0.5126
```


:::
:::


The proportions add up to 1 **within each species**, not overall. After `summarise()`, the result is still grouped by `species` (summarise removes only the *last* grouping variable), so `sum(n)` was computed per species. Three ways to be explicit:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1. remove the grouping
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   species   sex        n   prop
#>   <fct>     <fct>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie    female    73 0.2192
#> 2 Adelie    male      73 0.2192
#> 3 Chinstrap female    34 0.1021
#> 4 Chinstrap male      34 0.1021
#> 5 Gentoo    female    58 0.1742
#> 6 Gentoo    male      61 0.1832
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 2. drop groups inside summarise()
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(species, sex) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   species   sex        n   prop
#>   <fct>     <fct>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie    female    73 0.2192
#> 2 Adelie    male      73 0.2192
#> 3 Chinstrap female    34 0.1021
#> 4 Chinstrap male      34 0.1021
#> 5 Gentoo    female    58 0.1742
#> 6 Gentoo    male      61 0.1832
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# 3. use .by, which never leaves groups behind
penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(species, sex)) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   species   sex        n   prop
#>   <fct>     <fct>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 Adelie    male      73 0.2192
#> 2 Adelie    female    73 0.2192
#> 3 Gentoo    female    58 0.1742
#> 4 Gentoo    male      61 0.1832
#> 5 Chinstrap female    34 0.1021
#> 6 Chinstrap male      34 0.1021
```


:::
:::


Neither result is "wrong": proportions within species and proportions of the total answer **different questions**. The bug is getting one when you meant the other. When a tibble is grouped, its printout starts with a line like `# Groups: species [3]` — learn to look for it.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Forgetting `na.rm = TRUE`.** One missing value turns the mean, sd, min, max and sum into `NA`.
2. **Reporting `n()` as the sample size** when the variable has missing values. Use `sum(!is.na(x))` for the number of values actually used.
3. **Grouped data leaking into later steps.** After `group_by()`, every following `mutate()`, `summarise()` and `slice_*()` works by group. Use `.by`, `.groups = "drop"` or `ungroup()`.
4. **Using `mutate()` when you wanted `summarise()`** (or vice versa). `summarise()` gives one row per group; `mutate()` keeps every row.
5. **Comparing group means without looking at group sizes.** A mean based on 5 units is far less reliable than one based on 150; always report `n` next to it.
:::

## 7. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. How many rows does `penguins |> summarise(m = mean(bill_len, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(species, island))` return?

One per species–island combination **that exists in the data**: Adelie on three islands, Chinstrap on one, Gentoo on one — 5 rows.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. What is the difference between these two lines?

`penguins |> summarise(m = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)` and `penguins |> mutate(m = mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE), .by = species)`

The first returns 3 rows (one per species). The second returns all 344 rows, with the species mean repeated on each row.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. After `group_by(species, sex) |> summarise(n = n())`, by which variable is the result still grouped?

By `species`. `summarise()` drops only the last grouping variable (`sex`). Use `.groups = "drop"` to drop all of them.
:::

## 8. Exercises

### Interactive (run in your browser)


::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_10_1'}
```{webr}

penguins <- tibble::as_tibble(penguins)
```
:::


::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — summary by species.** For each species compute the median body mass, the standard deviation of body mass and the number of non-missing body mass values.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_10_1'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10_1
penguins |>
  summarise(
    median_mass = median(body_mass, ______),
    sd_mass     = ______,
    n_mass      = sum(!is.na(______)),
    .by = ______
  )
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_10_1"}
Every function needs `na.rm = TRUE`. Group with `.by = species`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_10_1"}
```r
penguins |>
  summarise(
    median_mass = median(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_mass     = sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_mass      = sum(!is.na(body_mass)),
    .by = species
  )
```
Gentoo has the highest median mass; the counts are 151 (Adelie), 123 (Gentoo) and 68 (Chinstrap).
:::
:::

```{webr}

penguins <- tibble::as_tibble(penguins)
```
:::


::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — `across()`.** Compute the mean of **all numeric measurements** except `year` (i.e. `bill_len`, `bill_dep`, `flipper_len`, `body_mass`) for each species, with column names like `bill_len_mean`.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_10_2'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10_2
penguins |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(bill_len:body_mass),
      list(mean = ______),
      .names = ______
    ),
    .by = species
  )
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_10_2"}
The function is `\(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; the name pattern is `"{.col}_{.fn}"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_10_2"}
```r
penguins |>
  summarise(
    across(
      c(bill_len:body_mass),
      list(mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    ),
    .by = species
  )
```
Chinstrap penguins have the longest bills on average (about 48.8 mm), Gentoo the shallowest (about 15.0 mm) but the longest flippers.
:::
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_10_3'}
```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_10_3
penguins <- tibble::as_tibble(penguins)
```
:::


::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug the proportions.** The goal is the proportion of penguins on each island **out of all penguins**, but the `prop` column is all ones. Why? Fix it.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_10_3'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10_3
penguins |>
  group_by(island) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  group_by(island) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_10_3"}
Inside each island group there is only one row, so `n / sum(n)` is always 1. Remove the second `group_by()` (or use `.by` in `summarise()`).
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_10_3"}
```r
penguins |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = island) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))
```
Biscoe hosts the largest share of the sample (about 49%), Torgersen the smallest (about 15%).
:::
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center" setup='true' exercise='ex_10_4'}
```{webr}

penguins <- tibble::as_tibble(penguins)
```
:::


::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — z-scores within species.** Add a column `z_mass` with the body mass standardised **within species**: subtract the species mean and divide by the species standard deviation. Then check that, within each species, `z_mass` has mean 0 and sd 1.


::: {.cell layout-align="center" exercise='ex_10_4'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_10_4
penguins |>
  mutate(
    z_mass = ______,
    .by = species
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_z = mean(z_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_z   = sd(z_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  )
```
:::


::: {.hint exercise="ex_10_4"}
`(body_mass - mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_10_4"}
```r
penguins |>
  mutate(
    z_mass = (body_mass - mean(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE)) /
      sd(body_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  ) |>
  summarise(
    mean_z = mean(z_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_z   = sd(z_mass, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = species
  )
```
The means print as 0 (or tiny numbers like `1e-16`, which are rounding errors) and the standard deviations as 1. A penguin with `z_mass = 2` is two standard deviations heavier than the average of *its own* species.
:::
:::

### Practice on your own computer

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — monthly ozone.** With `airquality`, compute for each `Month`: the mean `Ozone`, the number of days, the number of days with missing `Ozone` and the maximum `Temp`. Which month has the most missing ozone values? Why does this matter when comparing monthly means?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
airquality |>
  summarise(
    mean_ozone = mean(Ozone, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_days     = n(),
    n_missing  = sum(is.na(Ozone)),
    max_temp   = max(Temp),
    .by = Month
  )
```
June (`Month == 6`) has 21 missing ozone values out of 30 days, so its mean is based on only 9 days and is much less reliable than the others. If the missing days are not a random subset (for example, if the instrument failed on particular kinds of days), the June mean could also be biased — see [Missing data](../04-io/20-missing-data.qmd).
:::
:::

## Summary

| Tool | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `summarise()` | many rows → one row (per group) | `summarise(m = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))` |
| `n()`, `n_distinct()` | number of rows / of distinct values | `summarise(n = n(), k = n_distinct(g))` |
| `.by =` | group for one operation | `summarise(..., .by = c(g1, g2))` |
| `group_by()` | attach groups to the data | `group_by(g)`, then `summarise(...)` |
| `across()` | same function(s) on many columns | `across(where(is.numeric), list(mean = mean))` |
| grouped `mutate()` | group statistic on every row | `mutate(xc = x - mean(x), .by = g)` |
| `ungroup()`, `.groups = "drop"` | remove groups | `summarise(..., .groups = "drop")` |

- `summarise()` compresses, `mutate()` keeps every row: choose according to the question.
- Always use `na.rm = TRUE` deliberately, and report the number of non-missing values.
- Prefer `.by`: it groups for one step only and avoids leftover groups.
- Group summaries are the raw material of [descriptive statistics](../05-descriptive/22-summary-statistics.qmd) and of [comparisons between groups](../05-descriptive/23-two-variables.qmd).
